beats.text: An old man stands on trial for his life, accused of corrupting the young with questions.
The court offers Socrates a deal: stop philosophising, and live. He refuses.
"The unexamined life," he tells them, "is not worth living."
A life you never question — never tested, never understood — is barely your own, he says.
He claimed to know nothing. His only wisdom was that he knew he did not know.
They sentenced him to death. He drank the hemlock calmly, still arguing, unafraid.
So ask the dangerous question he died for: is the life you are living actually yours?

source_note: Quote: Plato's Apology, trans. Benjamin Jowett (public domain).
